<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but B consistently landed sharper, more damaging exchanges. A's core mechanism (fear silences victims/witnesses) is plausible but stayed abstract, and when pressed on falsifiability A could only gesture at unprovided metrics rather than substantiate the claim. B's concrete framing (known identity/known release time vs. field re-arrests) gave the debate a tangible cost that A never fully neutralized. The pivotal exchange was A's attempt to use B's notification concession as a "fatal" admission that the enforcement loss is merely a drafting flaw; B's answer—that policies must be judged "as enacted, not as redefined after failure"—directly turned that trap back on A and exposed that A's "narrow sanctuary" was an idealized version rather than the real-world ordinances B was indicting. A never adequately rebutted this reframe, and B got the last word reinforcing it. B's pressure questions (unfalsifiable benefit, hypocrisy on notification bans) also drew more damaging concessions than A's questions drew from B. A's opening being clipped is a minor execution cost. Overall B made the comparison easier to decide and left fewer open threads for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn 8 response to A's "notification fixes it" concession-trap ([B4.1]-[B4.3]), crystallized in B's closing line that policies must be judged "by what it enacts, not by the ideal version its defender invents after the bodies appear," most decisively reframed the debate in B's favor and went unanswered in A's final speech.</best_rebuttal>
